title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: A Mill-Town Childhood: Setting the Scene

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked — a close, passionate, and occasionally heated conversation about one of the great novels of the nineteenth century.
George Eliot published The Mill on the Floss in 1860, and it remains one of those novels that readers carry inside them for the rest of their lives.
It is the story of Maggie Tulliver — brilliant, ungovernable, hungry for a life bigger than her world will allow — and of the river that shapes, haunts, and ultimately claims her.
Today we are looking at how Eliot builds that world — the mill, the town, the family, the atmosphere — and how she uses narrative itself as a kind of memory.
I am joined by three extraordinary readers of this novel, and I want to introduce them properly.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novels on audio than almost anyone alive — he hears the rhythms of prose the way a conductor hears a score.
For a novel as obsessively concerned with voice and memory as this one, Oliver is exactly the reader we need.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished traditionalist critics in the country — he reads novels as moral tests of individual character, and he is magnificently suspicious of anything that smells like a programme.

And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads fiction as an anatomy of class and power — he tends to find the system lurking behind every apparently private drama, and he earns that reading with evidence.
Let us begin at the beginning — or rather, just before the beginning, because Eliot plays a remarkable trick in her very first pages.
Oliver, you have spent your professional life listening to narrators — what happens in that opening movement of The Mill on the Floss?
What happens is that Eliot pulls the rug out from under you — and does it with such warmth that you don't even mind.
She has spent several pages conjuring the mill, the river, the winter light — you are entirely inside this world — and then she says, in effect: I was asleep.
Here is how she puts it — and I want to read this exactly as written, because it is a perfect sentence.

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
That word — benumbed — is doing everything.
The body has been still so long it has gone numb — and that is precisely the condition of memory: a kind of willed, loving paralysis.

When I have read this aloud — and I have, many times — the audience always catches its breath at that moment, because the novel has just revealed its whole emotional strategy in a single domestic image.
Oliver is right to pause there, and I think it is worth saying precisely why that gesture is so daring.
Eliot has not merely broken the fictional frame — she has established that the entire novel exists inside a consciousness that loves what it is about to describe.
The novel begins as an act of devotion — a mind pressing itself against the arms of a chair so that it might hold on to a world that has passed.
That, I would argue, is the moral key to everything that follows — because the whole question of the novel is whether the past can be honoured without crushing the present.
I don't want to dispute that reading — I think it is genuinely true — but I want to add a dimension.

The world the narrator is dreaming of is not simply a personal past — it is a particular economic formation: a mill, a river, a provincial town organised around the wool trade and the mercantile family.
The nostalgia is real, but it is nostalgia for a specific class world that was already disappearing in 1860.
Eliot is not simply dreaming of her childhood — she is mourning a whole system of relations, and the novel will ask whose interests that system served.
And Eliot gives us a perfect portrait of that system — and its contradictions — in the figure of Mr. Glegg.
Mr. Glegg is one of my absolute favourite minor characters in all of Victorian fiction — the amiable skinflint, the man who saves other people's money with the same devotion he gives to his own.
But it is his bewilderment at Mrs. Glegg that produces Eliot's most perfectly timed comic prose.
She writes — and I savour every word of this —
"That a creature made — in a genealogical sense — out of a man's rib...should be normally in a state of contradiction to the blandest propositions and even to the most accommodating concessions."
"In a genealogical sense" — that parenthetical is a tiny masterpiece of satirical qualification.
Eliot is laughing at Mr. Glegg for invoking Genesis, and at Genesis for being invoked — all in four words.
The comedy is impeccable, but I think it conceals a serious moral portrait.
Mr. Glegg is not merely a comic type — he is a man who has made a genuine accommodation with life, who has found a way to be content within his own limitations.
Eliot is quite precise about this: his stinginess is, as she puts it, of the most amiable manner.
The satirical edge is there, but it is never cruel — and that restraint is, I think, the mark of a novelist who respects the people she is making fun of.
I want to press on that passage though, because what Eliot is actually anatomising is a specific economic psychology — the psychology of the provincial mercantile class.
She says explicitly that this habit of saving as an end in itself belonged to the industrious men of business of a former generation — it's a historical formation, not just a character quirk.
And she notes it is nearly lost in these days of rapid money-getting — she is writing at the exact hinge between these two worlds.
The Gleggs and the Dodsons are not just comic grotesques — they are the last representatives of a class fraction that capital is in the process of superseding.
And into this world — with all its thrift and its quarrelling and its damson cheese of venerable hardness — comes Tom Tulliver, who understands it perfectly and turns it to something almost noble.
There is a scene — Tom facing down his aunts after his father's ruin — where he speaks in the language of the family, the language of respectability and money, but redirects it entirely.
He says to Mrs. Glegg — and this is Tom at his most quietly devastating —
"Wouldn't it be better to give it now, and pay the debt we're going to be sold up for, and save my mother from parting with her furniture?"
He is using the Dodson logic — the horror of disgrace, the sacredness of furniture — and turning it against them.
It is a boy showing more moral intelligence than an entire roomful of adults.
That scene demonstrates something I think is central to Eliot's method — she builds a world of small social comedy, and then suddenly the stakes are real, and the characters must rise or fail.
Tom rises — imperfectly, rigidly, but he rises — and the comedy of the Gleggs and Dodsons is suddenly the backdrop to genuine moral action.
That movement — from comedy to moral seriousness — is one of the things Eliot does better than almost any other English novelist.
I agree with Edmund on this — though I would frame it differently.
What Tom is exposing is the gap between the Dodson ideology — family solidarity, respectability, honour — and the actual practice of that class when it costs them something.
He is calling the bluff of people for whom solidarity is a sentiment rather than a commitment — and the furniture, the sold-up furniture, is the material proof of their failure.
Eliot understands that the personal and the economic are never truly separable — and that insight runs all the way to the flood at the end.
And that flood — when it comes — is not simply a plot event.
Eliot has seeded it in the imagination from the very first pages — the river, the mill, the winter water — so that when Maggie is out on it in the dark, it feels both impossible and inevitable.
Listen to how Eliot connects flood to childhood nightmare — this is the passage I find most haunting in the entire novel.
"She was driven out upon the flood — that awful visitation of God which her father used to talk of; which had made the nightmare of her childish dreams."
"And with that thought there rushed in the vision of the old home, and Tom, and her mother — they had all listened together."
They had all listened together — four words that carry the entire weight of the childhood we have just spent several hundred pages inside.
The narrator who was dreaming at the start — pressing her elbows on the arms of a chair — has brought us all the way to this.
That is a remarkable place to pause — the dream that opened the novel materialising as catastrophe at its close.
We will be returning to Maggie and that flood — and to everything between the opening reverie and the final darkness.
But first, we need to go deeper into the world Eliot is dreaming of — the Tulliver household, the Dodsons, and the provincial world that made Maggie what she is and refused to make room for her.

segments.title: Maggie's Hunger: Intellect Against the Mill

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're turning our attention to Maggie Tulliver — the heart of this novel, and one of the most vividly imagined children in all of English fiction.
We're asking what it means to be hungry — intellectually, emotionally, spiritually — in a world that has no place for that hunger.
With me today are three guests who know this novel intimately and disagree about it productively.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic novel audiobooks than anyone alive — hears the music in Eliot's prose before he thinks about what it means.
Sir Edmund Leigh — Oxford don, moralist, and the sternest friend a novel could have — reads Maggie as a study in character tested by circumstance.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen — cultural historian and our sharpest reader of power — insists on asking who benefits from Maggie's suffering and why.
Let's begin at the beginning — with Maggie as a child, and with jealousy.
What I love about these early chapters — what I always come back to — is that Eliot doesn't sentimentalise the child.
Maggie is furious, she is petty, she is capable of genuine malice — and Eliot renders it with absolute fidelity.
There's that extraordinary moment when Tom starts paying attention to Lucy Deane, and something in Maggie simply curdles.
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
There's the comic timing right there — the white mouse is a masterstroke.
But then she goes on to tell us that Maggie was actually thinking about slapping Lucy, and pinching her — specifically to vex Tom.
That 'especially as it might vex Tom' — that's not a child being bad. That's a child being human.
Oliver is right that Eliot refuses sentimentality — but I think the more important word is 'demonstrable.'
What we are watching is the formation of a conscience — not a pretty conscience, but a real one.
Maggie feels things before she understands them, and her tragedy — her whole tragedy — is that she never quite catches up.
Later in the novel, when Tom confronts her about Philip Wakem, Eliot gives us this extraordinary anatomy of two defective moral natures.

"Tom had his terrible clutch on her conscience and her deepest dread; she writhed under the demonstrable truth of the character he had given to her conduct, and yet her whole soul rebelled against it as unfair from its incompleteness."
'Incompleteness' — that is the key word for both of them.
Tom's moral certainty is not wisdom — it is the refusal to examine himself. And Maggie's rebellion is not freedom — it is perpetual susceptibility.
I want to hold onto that word 'incompleteness' — but I'd put it differently.
What Maggie lacks is not self-knowledge. What she lacks is any legitimate outlet for what she knows about herself.
Look at what she does with her intelligence in childhood — she invents escape routes. Fantastical ones, but escape routes nonetheless.
After Tom rejects her, she doesn't sulk. She constructs an entire alternative social order.
"The resolution that gathered in her mind, after Tom and Lucy had walked away, was not so simple as that of going home."
She's going to the gypsies. And crucially — she expects them to respect her 'on account of her superior knowledge.'
That is a child who has been told her mind is too much and not enough — simultaneously — and who is trying to find one place in the world where it counts for something.
And then Eliot does something completely ruthless, which is let the fantasy play out — and let it collapse.
Maggie arrives among the gypsies and within minutes she has recast them entirely in her imagination.
The passage is pure gothic comedy — and I mean that as the highest praise.
Listen to this — she has begun to think
"that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
'Gradual cooking.' Two words. And the whole tragic-comic logic of Maggie's inner life is right there.
Her mind is so powerful that it destroys the very consolations it creates.
That is very finely put. Though I'd resist separating the comedy from the moral weight quite so cleanly.
What Eliot is tracing, through all these childhood episodes, is the development of a conscience that is at once too tender and too proud.
Her father understands this, I think, more than anyone. He sees her, but he cannot help her.
There is a moment of piercing simplicity when Mr. Tulliver says to her —
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
In eight words, Eliot delivers the whole weight of time and waste and irreversibility.
That is what great prose does — it does not explain; it makes you feel the thing itself.
I don't dispute the power of that line — it's devastating. But I want to note what Mr. Tulliver cannot say, even then.
He loves Maggie entirely. But the world he inhabits has no structure through which that love can be made useful to her.
She cannot inherit. She cannot be educated as Tom is educated. She cannot practise law or run a business or take any of the paths that would let her mind actually operate in the world.
And so that hunger — that enormous intellectual and emotional appetite — turns inward.
It finds Stephen Guest. It finds self-destruction. It finds the flood.
And Stephen's appeal to her — 'Call me back to life and goodness' — is the cruellest trap of all.
"Who besides me has met that long look of love that has burnt itself into my soul, so that no other image can come there?"
He is asking her to save him by sacrificing herself — which is precisely what every institution in her life has already demanded.
There's something almost operatic about that speech of Stephen's — the repetition, the escalating claims.
'Whose pain can have been like mine? Whose injury is like mine?' He's auditioning for his own suffering.
And yet — and this is where Eliot is so unsettling — we feel the pull of it. We understand why Maggie is not simply immune.
Her hunger is so acute that even a flawed, grandiose love like Stephen's carries the scent of something real.
What strikes me, listening to all three of you, is that Maggie's hunger is never satisfied — not in childhood, not in love, not in renunciation.
She is always reaching for something that the world around her — the mill, the town, the law, the men who love her — cannot provide.
In our next segment we'll turn to the world that produces and constrains her — the Dodson family, respectability, and the economics of ruin.

segments.title: The Tulliver Catastrophe: Economics and Dignity

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We turn now to the catastrophe at the heart of the novel — the Tulliver ruin, and everything it costs.
Not just money, but dignity, pride, and the peculiar honour of a man who cannot quite see himself clearly.
Oliver Trevelyan is here — the man who has voiced more classic novels than most of us have read, and who hears in Eliot's prose what the rest of us only dimly sense.
Sir Edmund Leigh joins us — the Oxford don who insists, with magnificent stubbornness, that novels are about character, not systems.
And Dr Daniel Rosen is with us — who reads the Tulliver disaster as an anatomy of class and power, and won't let us look away.
Let's begin with Mr Tulliver himself — a man careening toward ruin with something very like panache.
What I adore about Tulliver — and I have voiced him, so I speak with some authority — is that he is catastrophically, magnificently consistent.
He is heading for the rocks and he is doing so at full sail, colours flying.
Consider his letter to Mrs Glegg — written at the very moment the family is sliding into insolvency.
He tells her she needn't trouble her mind about her five hundred pounds, for it should be paid back in the course of the next month at farthest.
And then — and this is the touch of genius — he adds that she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.
He is repaying a debt he cannot afford in order to win an argument he has already lost.
That is not stupidity — that is a particular and terrible kind of pride, and Eliot renders it with complete comic sympathy.
Oliver puts his finger on the essential thing, though I might name it differently.
What Tulliver possesses — and what will destroy him — is a sense of honour that is entirely genuine, if fatally misapplied.
The letter to Mrs Glegg is not a comic letter.
It is the letter of a man who has decided that his independence matters more than his solvency.
One may call that folly — Dr Johnson would have called it exactly that — but there is a dignity in it that demands our respect alongside our exasperation.
The dignity is real — I won't dispute that.
But let's be precise about what kind of dignity it is, and what it costs.
Tulliver is a small property owner trapped between the Dodson commercial world above him and the grinding labour world below.
His honour is the honour of a man who cannot afford it — and the novel knows this even when Tulliver doesn't.
Mrs Glegg's five hundred pounds is not sentiment — it is leverage, credit, power within the family network.
When Tulliver renounces it, he thinks he is refusing condescension.
What he is actually doing is destroying his children's futures to preserve his own self-image.
That is somewhat brutal, Daniel, but I can't say it's wrong.
What Eliot is doing with Mrs Tulliver in these scenes is equally sharp, though in a more sideways fashion.
There is that extraordinary passage about the feather and the camel's back.
Mrs Tulliver's pleading might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back.
The narrator's parenthetical there — 'the credit or discredit' — is a tiny perfect joke and I relish it every time.
Eliot will not let even a simile pass without making it earn its place.
What strikes me in that passage is the extraordinary precision of the narrator's sympathy.
Mrs Tulliver is not powerful in herself — Eliot is quite clear about that.
Her influence operates because her husband sees in her the representative of the Dodson family.
He is not responding to her — he is fighting a symbolic battle that she happens to be standing in front of.
That is a very precise and painful observation about how marriage actually functions under certain conditions of male vanity.
And then there is Wakem.
Wakem is where this all becomes extraordinarily interesting from a structural point of view.
Tulliver is convinced — paranoid, but not entirely wrong — that Wakem is at the bottom of all his troubles.
He personalises what is actually a systemic phenomenon: the law serving property and capital against the small independent operator.
But listen to how Eliot renders his hatred — this is not mere resentment, it is a portrait of obsession.
A hook-nosed glib fellow — as cool as a cucumber — always looking so sure of his game!
That is free indirect speech at its most devastating — Tulliver's voice, but the narrator's scalpel.
And the bitter irony is that Tulliver has just been forced to take business to Wakem's office.
The system he hates has already made him its client.
The comedy of 'a hook-nosed glib fellow' is the comedy of absolute conviction — Tulliver knows exactly what Wakem is, and he is completely wrong, and also completely right.
There is something Dickensian in that portrait — the villain seen through the eyes of the man being destroyed by him.
The detail about Gore — Tulliver's own lawyer — being bald and round-featured with bland manners and fat hands — is a magnificent throwaway.
Tulliver needs a hawk and he has a pigeon.
I want to return to Daniel's point about the systemic, because I think it needs a small but important qualification.
The law does serve property — Daniel is right about that.
But what destroys Tulliver is not the law as such — it is his decision to use it.
The novel is absolutely unsparing on this point: Tulliver goes to law because his pride will not permit him not to.
The system is the river — but Tulliver is the man who wades in.
And now we come to what the ruin produces — not just debt, but a whole generation formed by it.
Eliot gives us a passage that I think is one of the most openly political things in the novel — and it is worth sitting with.
She is describing why unfashionable families require belief — require emphasis — in a way that good society simply does not.

Good society, floated on gossamer wings of light irony, is of very expensive production; requiring nothing less than a wide and arduous national life condensed in unfragrant deafening factories, cramping itself in mines, sweating at furnaces, grinding, hammering, weaving under more or less oppression of carbonic acid.
That sentence — in a Victorian novel — is an act of controlled fury.
Eliot is saying: your lightness is purchased with their suffering.
And the Tulliver family — ruined, struggling — are precisely among those whose emphasis of want funds good society's irony.
And out of that ruin comes Maggie's particular kind of renunciation — which is also rendered with devastating clarity.
Eliot says she threw some exaggeration and wilfulness, some pride and impetuosity, even into her self-renunciation.
Her own life was still a drama for her, in which she demanded of herself that her part should be played with intensity.
That is a young person's tragedy — performing suffering rather than enduring it.
And Eliot loves her for it, even as she diagnoses it with precision.
And then Tom.
Tom is the novel's most uncomfortable figure because his cruelty is never unmotivated — it always has logic.
In the confrontation with Philip Wakem, he deploys every weapon the damaged male ego has available to it.
Listen to what he actually says to Philip — there is no softening this.
I'll thrash you; I'll hold you up to public scorn. Who wouldn't laugh at the idea of your turning lover to a fine girl?
He weaponises Philip's deformity — the one thing Philip cannot answer, the one wound that cannot be defended.
And the ruin is the source of this: Tom has become the family's instrument of recovery, and he will brook no threat to that project, however human.
The Tulliver catastrophe does not end with the debts being paid — it ends in the children.
I find Tom Tulliver one of Eliot's most courageous portraits precisely because she refuses to make him merely villainous.
His speech to Philip — monstrous as it is — contains something that the novel itself acknowledges.
Earlier, Tom says to Maggie: I'll take care that the debts are paid, without your lowering yourself in that way.
The narrator notes — quietly, but firmly — that there was some tenderness and bravery mingled with the worldliness and self-assertion of that little speech.
Tom is not a monster — he is a damaged person performing the only virtue available to him.
Which, I would suggest, is precisely Mr Tulliver's tragedy played out in the next generation.
Pride inherited, dignity distorted, the system indifferent to all of it.
We've been tracing the Tulliver catastrophe from its comic origins in wounded pride all the way to its costs in the next generation.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to Maggie herself — her inner life, her reading, and the question of what it means to be a woman of extraordinary capacity in a world that has no use for it.

segments.title: Siblings in Collision: Tom, Maggie, and the Break

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been circling the great wound at the centre of this novel — the relationship between Tom and Maggie Tulliver.
In this segment we're going to look closely at how George Eliot builds that collision — passage by passage, year by year.
With me, as ever, are Oliver Trevelyan, Edmund Leigh, and Daniel Rosen.
Oliver brings the performer's ear — nobody hears the rhythms of a sibling quarrel on the page quite like he does.
Edmund reads character with the patience of a moralist — he'll hold us to what the novel actually says about goodness and will.
And Daniel reminds us that this family drama is never quite separable from the world of property, debt, and social exclusion pressing in on all sides.
Edmund, let's start with you — and with a passage from very early in the novel, before the great ruptures.
Eliot gives us a remarkable aside about the nature of childhood suffering — and a contrast between two fundamentally different kinds of mind.
What does that passage tell us about who these siblings actually are?
It tells us almost everything — and it tells us with a precision that I think is quite underrated.
The narrator has just shown us Maggie cutting off her own hair in a moment of desperate, impulsive rebellion.
And then Eliot draws back and gives us, quite deliberately, a philosophical portrait of two opposed temperaments.
Maggie rushes to her deeds with passionate impulse, as the narrator puts it, and then sees their consequences with agonising clarity.
Tom, by contrast, has — and this is a marvellous phrase — a wonderful instinctive discernment of what would turn to his advantage or disadvantage.
He doesn't reflect; he simply doesn't err in that direction.
But what strikes me most is the narrator's insistence that Maggie's anguish is not trivial.
She says — and I'd ask you to really hear this —

"Very trivial, perhaps, this anguish seems to weather-worn mortals who have to think of Christmas bills, dead loves, and broken friendships; but it was not less bitter to Maggie—perhaps it was even more bitter—than what we are fond of calling antithetically the real troubles of mature life."
That phrase — antithetically the real troubles — is an act of philosophical combat against adult condescension.
Eliot is saying: you are wrong to dismiss this child's pain, and here is why.
And there's a comic precision in the passage that I think we mustn't miss, even in all that pathos.
She sat as helpless and despairing among her black locks as Ajax among the slaughtered sheep.
Ajax among the slaughtered sheep — for a small girl who has cut her own hair!
That is Eliot at her most characteristic — the grandeur and the absurdity held in the same breath.
And the detail that keeps me: the apricot pudding and the custard.
If she had only let her hair alone, she could have sat with Tom and Lucy, and had the apricot pudding and the custard.
The specific, the material, the childishly real — that is how Eliot earns her philosophical digressions.
She plants the custard before she gives you the Homeric simile.
The contrast Eliot draws between Maggie and Tom is not merely temperamental — it is structural.
Tom has a wonderful instinctive discernment of what would turn to his advantage or disadvantage — Eliot's words.
That is not a moral virtue; that is a survival skill fitted to a world run on competition and self-interest.
Tom is being shaped, even in childhood, into the kind of man the commercial world rewards.
Maggie — imaginative, impulsive, unable to calculate — is being shaped into the kind of person it destroys.
And notice: it is Maggie who suffers the aunts' severe eyes, who loses the pudding, who weeps alone.
The punishment for not being Tom is immediate and social and material.
I take the point about the social dimension — but I'd resist the reduction.
Tom is not merely a creature of the market; he is a particular kind of moral agent — one who acts without remorse, who espoused his mistake and stood by it.
Eliot is quite precise here: Tom is wilful and inflexible in a way that has nothing to do with commerce.
It is a feature of his character — and character, in Eliot's moral universe, is the primary fact.
That portrait of Tom is thrown into sharp relief by what happens when he's taken out of his own element entirely — when he goes off to school under Mr Stelling.
Daniel, this passage has always struck me as one of the most quietly devastating things in the book.
What do we make of Tom humiliated by Latin and Euclid — and turning, in his desperation, to prayer?
It is devastating — and it is also an anatomy of how institutions break people.
Tom arrives at Stelling's with a pride quite comfortable in the world — the world of practical men, of mills and markets.
And that pride meets, as Eliot puts it, with nothing but bruises and crushings.
The Latin curriculum is not education; it is a class marker — a mechanism for sorting those who belong from those who don't.
And what does Tom do when the system defeats him entirely?
He prays — in the most heartbreaking, specific, transactional way imaginable.
Listen to the exactness of Eliot's rendering:
"and please to make me always remember my Latin."
That whisper contains the whole pathos of a boy trying to negotiate with God as he would negotiate with a schoolmaster.
And then — and this is the moment I love — he pauses to work out whether he should pray about Euclid separately.
Whether he should ask to see what it meant, or whether there was some other mental state more applicable to the case.
He approaches God with exactly the same methodical literalism he'd bring to a practical problem in the mill yard.
And yet — and this is where Eliot is so extraordinarily tender — it isn't comic.
Or rather, it is comic and it is unbearably moving at the same time.
We learn — almost in passing — that he has prayed for Maggie since she was a baby.
And then Euclid.
The tenderness and the comedy are inseparable — and that is the genius of it.
What strikes me here is the narrator's observation that Tom became more like a girl than he had ever been in his life before.
Eliot means by this that he acquired something of the girl's susceptibility — a sensitivity to judgment, to the approbation of others.
In other words: humiliation teaches Tom, briefly, what Maggie lives with as a permanent condition.
He glimpses her world — and his response is not compassion, but a more ferocious determination to return to his own.
And when Tom does return — when the family fortunes have collapsed and he reasserts himself as the authority in Maggie's life — the collision becomes explicit.
Oliver, you've been given the passage where Tom confronts Philip Wakem — the scene in the Red Deeps.
How do you read that speech?
Tom Tulliver speaks in that scene with the absolute certainty of a man who has never once doubted his own categories.
The prose of it is extraordinary — it sounds like the authentic voice of righteous fury rather than the voice of narration.
Here is what he says to Philip — and I want you to hear the rhythm of it, the way each charge lands:
"you—you to try and worm yourself into the affections of a handsome girl who is not eighteen, and has been shut out from the world by her father's misfortunes!"
"That's your crooked notion of honour, is it? I call it base treachery; I call it taking advantage of circumstances to win what's too good for you,—what you'd never get by fair means."
The word crooked — directed at a man with a physical deformity — is either the most brutal thing Tom could have said, or it is completely unconscious.
I have never been able to decide which — and I suspect Eliot intends that uncertainty.
It is not uncertainty — it is precisely Tom's character that makes it brutal either way.
His attack on Philip is structured entirely around what Philip can and cannot get by fair means.
That is the language of the market — of legitimate transaction and illegitimate advantage.
Tom has imported the logic of commercial honour entirely into the realm of human feeling.
Maggie is property to be protected, Philip is a debtor attempting fraud, and Tom is the bailiff of the family's moral estate.
I find Daniel's reading illuminating, but I think it mistakes the novel's own terms for those of a later critique.
Tom is wrong — Eliot is quite clear he is wrong — but his wrongness is a failure of imagination, not of ideology.
The narrator tells us — and this is a line I keep returning to —
"There was a terrible cutting truth in Tom's words,—that hard rind of truth which is discerned by unimaginative, unsympathetic minds."
Hard rind of truth — that is the novel's judgment on Tom, and it is more devastating than any Marxist account.
He is not wrong because the system has corrupted him; he is wrong because he is constitutionally incapable of sympathy.
And Maggie cannot refute him — that is the truly terrible thing.
The narrator says she rebelled and was humiliated in the same moment — because Tom holds a glass before her that shows her her own folly.
He functions as a kind of prophetic voice — predicting her future fallings with an accuracy that has nothing to do with love.
He is right about her conduct and wrong about everything that matters — and she knows both things simultaneously.
Edmund's point about imagination is well-taken — I won't abandon it, but I'll accept the refinement.
What I'd add is that the unimaginative mind is not distributed randomly in this novel — it tends to belong to those with something to protect.
Tom's narrowness is structural as well as personal; it is sustained and rewarded by the world he moves in.
Maggie's imaginative generosity, by contrast, makes her perpetually vulnerable — to her own impulses, to others' judgments, to the world's indifference.
And that vulnerability finds its most articulate expression in the novel's great scene of moral reckoning — when Maggie faces Stephen Guest and tries to explain what faithfulness actually requires.
Edmund, this passage has been called sentimental, it's been called heroic — where do you stand?
I stand firmly with the novel against its critics on this point.
The charge of sentimentality assumes that renunciation is easy — or that writing about it warmly is dishonest.
But listen to what Maggie actually says — and hear the philosophical precision beneath the emotion:
"Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves."
"They mean renouncing whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us,—whatever would cause misery to those whom the course of our lives has made dependent on us."
That is not a sentiment; that is a moral argument — carefully structured, philosophically serious.
And it comes from a woman who is also saying that she failed — that she was weak and selfish and hard.
This is the opposite of self-congratulation; it is the most demanding form of self-knowledge.
I don't dispute that Maggie's speech is morally serious — it plainly is.
But I want to ask: whose reliance is she honouring, and at what cost to herself?
The people Maggie names — Lucy, Philip — are both figures she has wronged precisely because the world allowed her so little room to live honestly.
She was shut out from the world by her father's misfortunes — Tom's own phrase — and it is that exclusion that makes clandestine affection possible, even inevitable.
When Maggie takes all the guilt upon herself, she is doing what the culture has trained her to do.
She internalises a judgment that should more properly fall on the world that confined her.
What undoes me in that passage — every time — is the cry about Lucy at the end.
Maggie has built this entire philosophical structure — faithfulness, constancy, renunciation — and then it breaks open:
"Oh, what is Lucy feeling now? She believed in me—she loved me—she was so good to me. Think of her——"
Those dashes at the end — think of her — are not vagueness; they are the limit of language.
The argument stops because grief stops it.
And that, to my mind, is worth ten pages of moral philosophy.
The argument stops because grief stops it — that feels like exactly the right place to pause in this segment.
We've traced the arc from the child weeping over her hair — from Maggie among the slaughtered sheep and the custard — all the way to this woman accounting for her own failure with terrible clarity.
What we've seen, I think, is that Tom and Maggie's collision is not an accident — it is written into them from the very beginning, by temperament and by circumstance.
After the break, we'll turn to how the novel imagines escape — and what it costs.
Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We're turning now to a subject that sits at the heart of the novel — the provincial world Eliot constructs, and what it actually costs the people who live inside it.
The St Ogg's community is drawn with tremendous affection, but also with tremendous precision about its cruelties.
Daniel Rosen has been thinking hard about the social architecture of this world — the way institutions, judgments, and even the warmth of belonging can function as forms of power.
Daniel, I want to begin with you, because I think you've found a tension in Eliot that some readers smooth over too quickly.
Thank you — yes, and I think it's a tension that goes all the way down into the novel's emotional structure.
Eliot is genuinely in love with the idea of home, of belonging, of the particular shapes that childhood presses into consciousness.
There's a passage early in the novel — Tom returning home from school — where the narrator opens up into something almost philosophical about that attachment.
That is one of the most beautiful defences of irrational attachment in the English novel.
But notice what Eliot is also doing — she's describing the mechanism by which a community holds its members.
The same roots that nourish you are what make it possible for St Ogg's to destroy Maggie.
I wouldn't quarrel with that reading, though I'd frame it rather differently.
What Eliot is describing in that passage is not a mechanism of social control — it is the precondition of any moral life at all.
Burke understood this perfectly — that the little platoon, the immediate circle of attachment, is where virtue is first formed and tested.
Eliot is not naive about St Ogg's — she sees its narrowness with perfect clarity.
But the novel's deepest claim is that character is forged in precisely these conditions, not in spite of them.
Maggie's tragedy is not that St Ogg's is provincial — it is that she outgrows it without anywhere larger to go.
That distinction — outgrowing without anywhere to go — is real, and I'd accept it.
But I want to push on the specific instrument of that destruction, which is Tom.
Tom is not simply narrow — he has absorbed and become St Ogg's moral code, and he delivers it with absolute conviction.
The passage where he turns Maggie away is one of the most shattering in Victorian fiction.
Every clause is a verdict — and every verdict is delivered in the language of community honour.
Tom is not evil — he is the community's most faithful representative, and that is precisely the indictment.
And yet Eliot does not let Tom off easily, but neither does she reduce him to a villain.
What is remarkable about that scene is that Tom believes, with complete sincerity, that he is doing his duty.
This is Eliot's great moral seriousness — she shows us that the capacity to do great harm and the capacity to act from genuine principle are not opposites.
Tom's fault is not dishonesty or cruelty for its own sake — it is rigidity, the inability to accommodate what exceeds the rule.
Eliot herself names this fault — she has a passage on precisely that moral limitation.
Yes — and that passage is, I think, the novel's most explicit statement of its own moral philosophy.
The narrator is talking about men of maxims — people who believe that moral judgment can be reduced to a set of portable rules.
Listen to how Eliot puts it — it's almost polemical in its directness.
That phrase — divine promptings — is doing enormous work.
Eliot is not arguing for sentimentality — she is arguing that genuine moral perception requires a kind of emotional and intellectual openness that rule-following forecloses.
Tom, with all his strength of will, has no access to that openness — and that, in the end, is why he cannot save his sister.
That is elegantly put, and I find myself largely in agreement.
Though I would note that Eliot's sympathy — the faculty she prizes above all others — is itself a form of discipline, not an escape from it.
She speaks of a hardly earned estimate of temptation — not feeling freely indulged, but feeling paid for with effort and understanding.
Maggie herself is tested on precisely this ground — her feelings are rich and her sympathy is real, but she is not always equal to the discipline they require.
That is not a failure of the novel — it is the novel's most honest achievement.
I want to return, before we move on, to the question of Philip Wakem — because he is, in some ways, the novel's most revealing figure.
He is excluded from the community by his deformity and his father's reputation — doubly marginalised.
And yet the narrator is extraordinarily precise about his psychology — including his capacity for self-deception.
There's a line in the passage about his feelings for Maggie that I find almost unbearably lucid.
There is the whole pathos of Maggie's situation, seen from outside — all that capacity for love, and nowhere to direct it.
Philip sees it clearly — but his clarity is also, as the narrator admits, entangled with his own desire to be that claim.
That image — wealth of love with no one to claim it — feels like a key to the whole novel.
The community that should receive that love has already decided who is and isn't entitled to give it.
We'll be exploring that exclusion further as we look at Maggie's own voice — and how she attempts to argue back against the world that has judged her.
Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the forces that shape — and ultimately break — Maggie Tulliver.

In this segment we're asking how the novel constructs Maggie's tragedy from within: through the natures of those around her, through the pull of childhood devotion, and through the dangerous lull of desire.
Sir Edmund Leigh has been sitting with three passages that seem to illuminate very different registers of that tragedy.
Edmund — where do you want to begin?
I want to begin with what I think is the most quietly devastating sentence in the whole of the novel's first half.
It concerns the friendship — if one can call it that — between Tom Tulliver and Philip Wakem.
Eliot reflects on why no lasting bond was possible between them, despite the genuine warmth of a shared moment of suffering.
She writes — and I think this deserves to be heard slowly —
"If boys and men are to be welded together in the glow of transient feeling, they must be made of metal that will mix, else they inevitably fall asunder when the heat dies out."
"The heat dies out."
That is the whole of it, isn't it.
What strikes me about that image — the welding, the incompatible metals — is that it's a blacksmith's metaphor in the mouth of a philosopher.
Eliot doesn't reach for something refined or classical.
She reaches for the forge.
And there's something embedded just before that sentence that I find wonderfully mordant — Mr Tulliver's little warning about Philip.
He says, setting up the whole poisoning of Tom's mind:
"Ay, ay, the gray colt may chance to kick like his black sire."
A proverb from the stables, and it does all the damage Wakem himself ever could.
And notice who delivers that proverb: the father, in the very act of telling Tom to be kind.
The prejudice is transmitted through the warmth, not in spite of it.
That is how class hatred reproduces itself — wrapped in the idiom of folk wisdom, delivered at the hearth.
Tom has no chance, really.
I wouldn't quite call it class hatred, Daniel.
Tulliver's distrust of Wakem is personal, historical, rooted in grievance.
What Eliot is showing us, I think, is something rather more uncomfortable: that incompatibility of nature is real, and no amount of goodwill can dissolve it.
The metal simile isn't a social diagnosis — it's a moral one.
And this brings us rather naturally to Maggie herself — to what I'd call the emotional centre of your second passage, Edmund.
The moment Maggie sees her father diminished — helpless — and everything else falls away.
Yes — and here the narrator moves from the diagnostic to something almost sacramental.
We are told this is one of those supreme moments when everything Maggie has hoped for or dreaded falls away.
Eliot describes it as:
"that simple, primitive love which knits us to the beings who have been nearest to us, in their times of helplessness or of anguish."
"Simple" and "primitive" — not used dismissively, but with great reverence.
This is Eliot saying: beneath all the intellectual striving, beneath all the hunger for something more, there is this.
The phrase "knits us" does something very particular, doesn't it.
It's domestic — almost homely — but it binds absolutely.
You can't unknit what has been knitted together through someone's suffering.
And for Maggie, that bond with her father is precisely what makes her later choices so impossible.
She is knit to the past before she has any say in the matter.
The passage also says something about age and vulnerability that I find arresting: "Poor child!"
The narrator is watching Maggie enter a kind of emotional knowledge that is genuinely too large for her.
"It was very early for her to know one of those supreme moments in life."
She is formed by grief before she is formed by anything else.
And the novel — quietly, systematically — shows us how that formation becomes the instrument of her destruction.
Which leads us, with a kind of terrible logic, to the boat.
The passage on the river with Stephen Guest — Edmund, you've been living with this one.
There are passages in this novel of such beauty that criticism feels almost impertinent.
This is one of them.
Eliot renders the drift downriver in prose that is itself drifting:
"The breath of the young, unwearied day, the delicious rhythmic dip of the oars, the fragmentary song of a passing bird heard now and then, as if it were only the overflowing of brimful gladness —"
One long accumulating breath, and you are already in the boat with them.
But the narrator also tells us that Maggie "dwelt with no recognition on the villages" — she has stopped noticing her waymarks.
That is the tragedy coiled inside the beauty.
The sentence that gets me every time is the one about thought.
Eliot writes — and I almost want to whisper this —
"what could words have been but an inlet to thought? and thought did not belong to that enchanted haze in which they were enveloped."
Words lead to thought, and thought leads to the past and the future — and both of those are catastrophic.
So silence is the only way the moment can survive.
It's a gorgeous trap, and Eliot springs it with complete deliberateness.
The word I keep returning to in that passage is "automatically."
Stephen rows "half automatically" — he too has surrendered agency.
But the novel is not symmetrical about this.
It is Maggie who will bear the social cost of what happens on this river.
Stephen will be embarrassed; she will be destroyed.
That is true — and it is precisely the point Eliot is building toward.
But I'd resist the implication that Eliot merely indicts a social structure.
What the passage also shows is that Maggie is genuinely complicit in her own enchantment.
She knows the waymarks are passing.
She chooses not to see them.
That choice — or its absence — is at the heart of what makes Maggie so enduring and so heartbreaking as a character.
We'll carry that question — of constraint, complicity, and what the novel finally asks of its heroine — into the next part of our discussion.

segments.title: The Flood and the Self: Eliot's Tragic Vision

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracking the great currents of The Mill on the Floss — character, society, moral imagination, the weight of the past on the living.
Before we close, I want to return to the world Eliot built with such precision — particularly the Dodson tradition, that dense social fabric from which Maggie can never quite free herself.
Edmund, you've been our guide to the moral and social architecture of the novel. What does Eliot's treatment of the Dodsons tell us about her tragic vision?
One must begin, I think, by resisting the temptation to caricature the Dodsons.
Eliot is a satirist of extraordinary precision, but she is never merely a satirist.
Consider how she characterises the Dodson religion — and here the prose is quite remarkable.

"Their religion was of a simple, semi-pagan kind, but there was no heresy in it,—if heresy properly means choice,—for they didn't know there was any other religion, except that of chapel-goers, which appeared to run in families, like asthma."
That parenthetical — 'if heresy properly means choice' — is Eliot at her most devastating.
These people are not wicked. They are, in a profound sense, unchosen — they have never stood at any crossroads of belief.
And that is precisely the world against which Maggie's restless, choosing nature must break itself.
Edmund puts his finger on something essential, and I want to push a little further into the comedy — because the comedy is load-bearing.
There's a passage about the Dodson women visiting strange houses — meaning anyone else's house — that I find almost unbearably funny.
"A female Dodson, when in 'strange houses,' always ate dry bread with her tea, and declined any sort of preserves, having no confidence in the butter."
'No confidence in the butter.' That is a sentence I would have given a great deal to have written.
But the real genius is this: Mrs Tulliver is described as 'a thorough Dodson, though a mild one, as small-beer, so long as it is anything, is only describable as very weak ale.'
Eliot builds an entire taxonomy of provincial character from the quality of the butter and the strength of the beer.
That is not mockery. That is a novelist in absolute command of her material.
I want to hold on to what Edmund and Oliver have both said, and think about what the Dodson code actually does as a social mechanism.
Eliot says their pride consisted in 'the utter frustration of all desire to tax them with a breach of traditional duty or propriety.'
That is not simply a personality trait. That is a class strategy.
'To be honest and poor was never a Dodson motto, still less to seem rich though being poor; rather, the family badge was to be honest and rich.'
The Dodsons police themselves, police their kin, police Maggie — in the name of tradition. But the tradition exists to protect property.
And Maggie's tragedy is not just psychological — it's that she cannot be accommodated within a social order structured entirely around inheritance and respectability.
Daniel is right about the property, but I think he undersells Eliot's sympathy for these values — not merely her irony.
Eliot says — and she means it — that 'society owes some worthy qualities in many of her members to mothers of the Dodson class.'
Industry, faithfulness to kin, rigid honesty, thoroughness of work — these are not trifling virtues.
The tragedy of the novel is not that the Dodsons are villains but that their genuine virtues are too rigid to accommodate a spirit like Maggie's.
And then there is Mr Tulliver — who is, let's be honest, the great comic-tragic engine of the first half of the book.
Eliot's diagnosis of his character is, I think, one of the most penetrating things in the novel.

"It is really not improbable that there was a direct relation between these apparently contradictory phenomena, since I have observed that for getting a strong impression that a skein is tangled there is nothing like snatching hastily at a single thread."
The skein and the thread — that is a metaphor for Tulliver's entire life, and for every lawsuit he ever drew himself into.
A man who sees complexity clearly in quiet moments, and then snaps at the first loose thread the moment feeling runs high.
That passage on Tulliver also points to something about the novel's structural irony — which is worth naming directly.
Tulliver's ruin is not caused by capitalism in any abstract sense. It is caused by his own psychology meeting a legal and financial system that rewards exactly the opposite of how he operates.
He borrows, he lends to Moss, he snatches at threads — and the law, which is patient and technical, destroys him.
And what I find remarkable is that Eliot extends this same sympathy to Maggie — whose mind is also a tangle of acuity and blind spots.
The narrator says of young Maggie that 'her thoughts generally were the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams.'
Father and daughter: both operating beyond the coordinates their world has prepared them to navigate.
That connection between Tulliver and Maggie is the heart of the novel, I believe.
And the passage on Maggie's education is one Eliot delivers with a kind of tender comedy that is entirely her own.
She had read the dictionary. She had deduced that 'poly' means 'many.' She knew the word 'polygamy.'
And yet, as the narrator tells us, 'in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge.'
'Her small mind.' That phrase is devastating in context — not condescending, but heartbreaking.
Because Eliot is describing the constraints of a world that has given this remarkable child almost nothing — and watching her build cathedrals from the rubble.
Cathedrals from rubble — I shall be quoting Edmund for years.
What strikes me, returning to these passages, is how insistently comic the surface of this novel is — even when the undertow is pulling toward catastrophe.
The Dodsons with their dry bread, Tulliver on his horse riding off to make things worse, little Maggie and her dictionary — Eliot is funny on almost every page.
And then the flood. And then silence.
That contrast — laughter and catastrophe, the ordinary and the devastating — may be the most Eliot thing of all.
Oliver Trevelyan, Edmund Leigh, Daniel Rosen — thank you for a conversation that has done full justice to a novel that demands and rewards exactly this kind of care.

The Mill on the Floss remains, one hundred and sixty years on, one of the most searching novels in the English language — about family, about class, about the terrible cost of being the kind of person who cannot help but feel and think too much.
We hope you'll carry it with you. Thank you for listening to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

c12:p6.text:
Mr Glegg on his side, too, had a double source of mental occupation, which
gave every promise of being inexhaustible. On the one hand, he surprised
himself by his discoveries in natural history, finding that his piece of
garden-ground contained wonderful caterpillars, slugs, and insects, which, so
far as he had heard, had never before attracted human observation; and he
noticed remarkable coincidences between these zoological phenomena and the
great events of that time,—as, for example, that before the burning of
York Minster there had been mysterious serpentine marks on the leaves of the
rose-trees, together with an unusual prevalence of slugs, which he had been
puzzled to know the meaning of, until it flashed upon him with this melancholy
conflagration. (Mr Glegg had an unusual amount of mental activity, which, when
disengaged from the wool business, naturally made itself a pathway in other
directions.) And his second subject of meditation was the
“contrairiness” of the female mind, as typically exhibited in Mrs
Glegg. That a creature made—in a genealogical sense—out of a
man’s rib, and in this particular case maintained in the highest
respectability without any trouble of her own, should be normally in a state of
contradiction to the blandest propositions and even to the most accommodating
concessions, was a mystery in the scheme of things to which he had often in
vain sought a clew in the early chapters of Genesis. Mr Glegg had chosen the
eldest Miss Dodson as a handsome embodiment of female prudence and thrift, and
being himself of a money-getting, money-keeping turn, had calculated on much
conjugal harmony. But in that curious compound, the feminine character, it may
easily happen that the flavour is unpleasant in spite of excellent ingredients;
and a fine systematic stinginess may be accompanied with a seasoning that quite
spoils its relish. Now, good Mr Glegg himself was stingy in the most amiable
manner; his neighbours called him “near,” which always means that
the person in question is a lovable skinflint. If you expressed a preference
for cheese-parings, Mr Glegg would remember to save them for you, with a
good-natured delight in gratifying your palate, and he was given to pet all
animals which required no appreciable keep. There was no humbug or hypocrisy
about Mr Glegg; his eyes would have watered with true feeling over the sale of
a widow’s furniture, which a five-pound note from his side pocket would
have prevented; but a donation of five pounds to a person “in a small way
of life” would have seemed to him a mad kind of lavishness rather than
“charity,” which had always presented itself to him as a
contribution of small aids, not a neutralizing of misfortune. And Mr Glegg was
just as fond of saving other people’s money as his own; he would have
ridden as far round to avoid a turnpike when his expenses were to be paid for
him, as when they were to come out of his own pocket, and was quite zealous in
trying to induce indifferent acquaintances to adopt a cheap substitute for
blacking. This inalienable habit of saving, as an end in itself, belonged to
the industrious men of business of a former generation, who made their fortunes
slowly, almost as the tracking of the fox belongs to the harrier,—it
constituted them a “race,” which is nearly lost in these days of
rapid money-getting, when lavishness comes close on the back of want. In
old-fashioned times an “independence” was hardly ever made without
a little miserliness as a condition, and you would have found that quality in
every provincial district, combined with characters as various as the fruits
from which we can extract acid. The true Harpagons were always marked and
exceptional characters; not so the worthy tax-payers, who, having once pinched
from real necessity, retained even in the midst of their comfortable
retirement, with their wallfruit and wine-bins, the habit of regarding life as
an ingenious process of nibbling out one’s livelihood without leaving any
perceptible deficit, and who would have been as immediately prompted to give up
a newly taxed luxury when they had had their clear five hundred a year, as when
they had only five hundred pounds of capital. Mr Glegg was one of these men,
found so impracticable by chancellors of the exchequer; and knowing this, you
will be the better able to understand why he had not swerved from the
conviction that he had made an eligible marriage, in spite of the too pungent
seasoning that nature had given to the eldest Miss Dodson’s virtues. A
man with an affectionate disposition, who finds a wife to concur with his
fundamental idea of life, easily comes to persuade himself that no other woman
would have suited him so well, and does a little daily snapping and quarrelling
without any sense of alienation. Mr Glegg, being of a reflective turn, and no
longer occupied with wool, had much wondering meditation on the peculiar
constitution of the female mind as unfolded to him in his domestic life; and
yet he thought Mrs Glegg’s household ways a model for her sex. It struck
him as a pitiable irregularity in other women if they did not roll up their
table-napkins with the same tightness and emphasis as Mrs Glegg did, if their
pastry had a less leathery consistence, and their damson cheese a less
venerable hardness than hers; nay, even the peculiar combination of grocery and
druglike odors in Mrs Glegg’s private cupboard impressed him as the only
right thing in the way of cupboard smells. I am not sure that he would not have
longed for the quarrelling again, if it had ceased for an entire week; and it
is certain that an acquiescent, mild wife would have left his meditations
comparatively jejune and barren of mystery.
c12:p6.summary: Mr Glegg finds mystery in caterpillars and slugs while remaining bewildered by his wife's contradictions; he practices amiable thrift and loves order, having married for conjugal harmony but finding seasoning that spoils the relish.

The whole thing had been so rapid, so dreamlike, that the threads of ordinary
association were broken; she sank down on the seat clutching the oar
mechanically, and for a long while had no distinct conception of her position.
The first thing that waked her to fuller consciousness was the cessation of the
rain, and a perception that the darkness was divided by the faintest light,
which parted the overhanging gloom from the immeasurable watery level below.
She was driven out upon the flood,—that awful visitation of God which her
father used to talk of; which had made the nightmare of her childish dreams.
And with that thought there rushed in the vision of the old home, and Tom, and
her mother,—they had all listened together.

Maggie said nothing, but turned away from her with a deeper frown. As long as
Tom seemed to prefer Lucy to her, Lucy made part of his unkindness. Maggie
would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty
little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but
then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been
left to Maggie to pet and make much of her. As it was, she was actually
beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or
pinching her, especially as it might vex Tom, whom it was of no use to slap,
even if she dared, because he didn’t mind it. And if Lucy hadn’t
been there, Maggie was sure he would have got friends with her sooner.

c37:p64.text:
Not a word was spoken as they walked along. Maggie was suffering in
anticipation of what Philip was about to suffer, and dreading the galling words
that would fall on him from Tom’s lips; but she felt it was in vain to
attempt anything but submission. Tom had his terrible clutch on her conscience
and her deepest dread; she writhed under the demonstrable truth of the
character he had given to her conduct, and yet her whole soul rebelled against
it as unfair from its incompleteness. He, meanwhile, felt the impetus of his
indignation diverted toward Philip. He did not know how much of an old boyish
repulsion and of mere personal pride and animosity was concerned in the bitter
severity of the words by which he meant to do the duty of a son and a brother.
Tom was not given to inquire subtly into his own motives any more than into
other matters of an intangible kind; he was quite sure that his own motives as
well as actions were good, else he would have had nothing to do with them.
c37:p64.summary: Maggie suffers in anticipation of Philip's suffering and Tom's cruel words; she feels Tom's moral leverage over her conscience but rebels against his characterisation as incomplete and unfair. Tom, unaware of his own boyish repulsion and personal pride underlying his severity, is convinced his motives are good because he would not otherwise engage in them.
